R50 supplies GAP code in place of a proof and states as much (0.636/0.019). R51 gives a base-60 halving procedure with four worked cases and a practice problem (0.981/0.151). R48 closes by pointing at theorem 12.29 of Rudin (0.874/0.170), and R01 supplies three DOIs (0.772/0.129). Every one of these is deep in the scorecard's bottom quartile. Cited: R16, R50, R51, R48.

proposals.name: Extends to the neighbouring cases the asker will meet next
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer, after settling the question, equips the asker for the adjacent cases: states the general rule the specific answer instantiates, checks a nearby variant, explains why the obvious alternative route fails, or poses a companion instance for the asker to try. 10 = present and genuinely adjacent to the asker's situation. 5 = a generic closing remark about generality. 0 = the specific case is settled and nothing transfers, or the generalization offered is aimed at a different audience than the asker.
proposals.rationale: Several dense-high, card-low items do exactly this and nothing a rigour bank would score. R51 works the general base-b claim, then asks 'You try one: What is 9:51 divided by two?' and answers it (dense 0.981, card 0.151). R05, having settled 9!, immediately checks 10!, 7! and 8! and finds the same value (0.834/0.009). R08 pauses to explain why the natural $k$-nary map fails and the $(k+1)$-nary one does not (0.807/0.144), and R53 answers the notation question and then lays out the field axioms that make $k^\times$ worth its own symbol (0.991/0.344). Cited: R51, R05, R08, R53.

proposals.name: Presupposes other answers already exist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer text presupposes that other answers or comments to this same question already exist before it. Count explicit openers and asides such as 'another approach', 'yet another way', 'an alternate approach', 'here is a second/other answer', 'the other answer(s)...', 'this is a complement to X's answer', 'I post this answer separately', 'expanding on a comment', 'the other answers are way too complicated', 'I just wanted to add'. 0 = the text engages the raw question from scratch with no sign that anything has been said yet; 10 = the answer is framed throughout as an addition, alternative, correction, or complement to material already present on the page. Do NOT judge whether framing an answer this way is good, modest, useful, or bad; score only how much of this presupposition language is visible.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3. This is a pure position fingerprint: a later arrival can see what is already posted and says so, while a first arrival cannot. R03 opens 'Another approach based on a theorem...', R16 opens 'The other answer has roughly the right idea', R31 opens 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to the Robert Israel's answer', R59 opens 'The other answers are way too complicated for this particular problem', R49 opens 'I post this answer separately'; by contrast R01, R06 and R33 start cold on the mathematics. Arrival order is not the asker's judgement of the answer, yet it is strongly legible in the text and plausibly co-varies with how items fare, so it must be discounted. Tagged mixed because a late answerer who has read the others may genuinely add something the earlier ones lacked.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the answer stream (arrival order relative to other answers)

proposals.name: Era-marked macro and markup dialect
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text uses site-era-marked or personal-macro typesetting dialect rather than plain modern MathJax. Look for: inline \newcommand / \def preambles at the top of the answer (e.g. \def\QQ{\mathbb{Q}}, \newcommand{\O}{\mathcal{O}}, home-rolled environment macros), the short \Bbb and \frak forms instead of \mathbb and \mathfrak, hand-built array/ascii layout used to simulate structure, \tag/\label/\eqref cross-referencing, and old-style spellings of theorem names without accents (Poincare, Schroder). 0 = none of these, plain default markup only; 10 = several such dialect features, including a macro preamble. Do NOT judge whether the markup is elegant, correct, or well chosen; score only how much era/dialect-marked machinery is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 (position in the site's own history). Notation fashions on math.SE shift over time and \def preambles were far more common in some eras than others, so this is a clock, not a property of the answer's fit to the asker's need. R46 opens with a six-macro \def preamble, R40 uses \newcommand{\O}{\mathcal{O}}, R54 defines a whole \fitch macro, R07 writes $\Bbb N$ and $2^\frak{c}$, R02 and R30 write 'Poincare' and 'Schroder' unaccented, while R01, R12 and R33 carry no dialect markers at all. A judge can score the trace without knowing the year.
proposals.upstream_parent: era of the site the answer was written in, and the author's accumulated markup habit

proposals.name: Second-person coaching addressed at the asker
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer is written AT the person who asked rather than at a general future reader. Count: direct second-person address about the asker's own work ('your computation', 'your work is correct', 'you are overcomplicating it', 'there may be some little mistakes in your computation', 'in your case'), instructions handed to the asker ('now you can solve for x', 'you just need to show', 'I'll leave the last step to you', 'you try one'), quoting the asker's own words back, and encouragement or sign-offs aimed at one person ('I hope this was helpful', 'Cheers!'). 0 = no second-person address, written impersonally for anyone who lands on the page; 10 = sustained one-to-one coaching register throughout. Do NOT judge whether addressing the asker directly is helpful, patronising, or appropriate; score only how much of it is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 and MODE 4. The unseen factor is who the writer imagines reading; the textual fingerprint is person and mood. R12 ends 'So your work is correct', R17 opens 'You are overcomplicating it' and signs '-Shahar', R43 says 'You are lucky here' plus a 'PS:' aimed at the asker, R44 quotes the asker's question back in quotation marks, R28 sets the asker an exercise ('You try one'), R52 is entirely 'if you are enumerating... you need to multiply'; against these R02, R40 and R60 never address anyone. Audience conception is upstream of the text and not itself the asker's selection. Tagged mixed because writing for the specific asker may also genuinely serve that asker.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's conception of their audience (this asker versus future searchers)

proposals.name: Typeset formal machinery versus running prose
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item consists of typeset mathematical machinery rather than ordinary sentences. Estimate the share of the text occupied by display equations, align/split/array environments, chains of numbered or tagged equations, and formal apparatus headers ('Lemma 1.', 'Claim 2', 'Proof', 'Definition:', 'Case 1.'), as opposed to running natural-language explanation. 0 = essentially all prose with at most an inline symbol; 10 = essentially all display blocks and formal headers with only connective fragments between them. Do NOT judge whether the mathematics is correct, whether the formality is warranted, or whether prose would have been better; score only the proportion of typeset machinery.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1. A crude layout statistic any tokenizer-level model can latch onto. R01 is a single align block with a four-word lead-in, R06 and R08 are near-continuous align/split chains, R50 is one enormous align plus a reference list, while R18, R20 and R32 are almost pure prose with a handful of inline symbols, and R48 is dense Lemma/Proof apparatus. The proportion tracks the subject area and the writer's habit, not the asker's choice, so it should be a declared nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Sheer bulk and sprawl of the answer
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of the answer's bulk and sprawl. Consider: total length, number of paragraphs, number of distinct stages or sub-arguments, presence of multiple parallel viewpoints or appendices, whether the text runs on past a natural stopping point, and whether it appears to be cut off mid-sentence or mid-word because it exceeded a display limit. 0 = one or two sentences or a single short block; 10 = many screens of continuously developing material, possibly truncated at the end. Do NOT judge whether the length is justified, thorough, bloated, or lazy; score only how much text there is.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1, the canonical verbosity proxy. The slice spans nearly the full range: R45 is two sentences, R47 is one line, R10 is a single 'Hint:' clause and R11 is a three-line counterexample, whereas R42, R46, R25 and R57 run to many paragraphs and are visibly truncated mid-word. Length is upstream of both models and is measurable without reading for sense, so it is exactly the sort of channel that can carry apparent predictive power for reasons unrelated to the asker's selection. Tagged mixed because a longer answer sometimes does contain genuinely more of what the asker wanted.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Names other site participants by handle or first name
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text refers to other identifiable people on the site by name, handle, or role. Count: first names and usernames of other answerers or commenters ('as suggested by Ted', "Clive's answer", 'a comment by Bill', 'as Dilip points out', '@supinf showed us', 'Semiclassical got there first', 'now validated by Prof. Shifrin', 'To @ Asaf Shachar'), the site abbreviation 'OP' used to denote the asker, and references to the writer's own earlier posts ('my 2011 answer', 'my first post', 'my other solution below'). 0 = no person is named or referenced; 10 = several named participants and/or repeated self-reference to the writer's own back catalogue. Do NOT judge whether crediting others is generous, correct, or self-promoting; score only how much naming is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. A regular knows the other regulars and the local vocabulary ('OP'), and says so; a stranger cannot. The trace is visible even though the reputation behind it is not. R02 credits 'as suggested by Ted', R22 opens "Clive's answer is already a good one", R29 opens 'This is expanding on a comment by Bill', R35 says 'as Dilip points out', R58 opens '@supinf showed us', R49 says 'Semiclassical got there first', R46 cites 'my 2011 answer', R09 and R31 use 'OP' and name Robert Israel; R01, R33 and R39 name nobody. Standing is not the asker's judgement of this answer, so the fingerprint must be discounted. Tagged mixed because embedded regulars may also write better-targeted answers.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's standing and embeddedness in the site community (a known regular versus a first-time poster)

proposals.name: Flat declarative terseness versus visible hedging
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text is flatly declarative and unhedged. High scores: bare assertions with no epistemic softening, one-line verdicts, imperative 'Hint:' or 'Note that' openings, closing markers of finality ('Done!', 'qed', 'q.e.d.', $\blacksquare$, 'This is not possible', 'Conclusion: ...none'). Low scores: visible hedging and self-qualification ('I think', 'if I remember right', 'the following might work', 'imho', 'this might help', 'I don't have a written proof', 'the third and fourth are discutable', 'maybe the most natural choice', 'I get a proof as follows'). Score 10 for wholly unhedged, 0 for pervasively hedged. Do NOT judge whether the confidence is warranted or whether hedging is honest; score only the register.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 and MODE 4. Register is a habit acquired by writing many answers, not a property of this answer's fit to the question. Unhedged end of the slice: R60 'This is not possible', R11 'but clearly B != C', R47 'So, we have at least 5+35=40', R39 'Done!', R06 closing with $\blacksquare$, R02 closing 'qed', R10 a bare 'Hint:'. Hedged end: R29 'if I remember right' and 'the following might work', R38 "I don't have a written proof", R51 'I think it is important to state', R20 'imho', R31 'The third and fourth are discutable', R48 'Based on the iead of proving Lyapunov's theorem'. Tagged mixed because a practised answerer may both write tersely and actually know more.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's practice and seniority in this format (a practised regular's willingness to be terse and flatly declarative)

proposals.name: Visible post-hoc editing and appended layers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text shows visible signs of having been revised or extended after it was first posted. Count: literal edit markers ('EDIT', 'EDIT 1.', 'EDIT 2.', 'Edit:'), appended afterthought sections ('Note:', 'Important Note:', 'PS:', 'Disclaimer', 'Answer at end' followed later by the answer), replies to named commenters embedded in the body ('To @ Asaf Shachar', '(Please see comment below for more info on these diagrams)', 'now validated by Prof. Shifrin'), retractions or corrections of the writer's own earlier lines, and pointers to the writer's other posts on the same question. 0 = a single uninterrupted composition; 10 = several clearly layered accretions. Do NOT judge whether revising was diligent or whether the additions improve the answer; score only how much layering is visible.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Editing happens after submission, in response to on-page discussion, so it is downstream of process rather than of the answer's original content; but it leaves an unmistakable textual trace. R56 carries 'EDIT 1. (To Asaf Shachar)' and 'EDIT 2. To @ Asaf Shachar', R29 has a bare 'EDIT' before the long calculation, R59 has 'Edit:' followed by 'or I'll just do it for you myself, since you seem to think...', R49 appends a 'Disclaimer' paragraph, R35 appends 'Note: my other solution below is much quicker', R57 opens 'now validated by Prof. Shifrin', R28 appends 'Important Note:'. Nothing comparable appears in R01, R11 or R33. Tagged mixed because an answer that was patched in response to objections may end up genuinely more complete.
proposals.upstream_parent: post-submission process dynamics (comment exchange and subsequent editing after the item was first posted)

proposals.name: Routine drill versus specialist-topic question genre
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item sits at the specialist/research-flavoured end of the subject spectrum rather than the routine-exercise end. Score high for advanced or graduate vocabulary and objects in the question and answer (forcing, generic filters, Galois groups and cyclotomic fields, fibre bundles and Poincare-Hopf, sheaf/category-theoretic diagrams, spectral theorem on manifolds, Bell polynomials), and for questions that are conceptual or 'why' shaped. Score low for standard first-course drill: simplify this expression, differentiate this, evaluate this limit, solve this inequality, find the max/min, and especially for signs the item is a multiple-choice textbook item (answer options, 'Option (A) is correct', boxed final numeric answer). 0 = plainly routine exercise; 10 = plainly specialist research-adjacent material. Do NOT judge whether harder questions or their answers are better; score only where the subject matter sits.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 and MODE 2. The genre of the question controls how many answers compete, who shows up, and how the page behaves, all upstream of any single answer's text, yet the genre is fully legible from vocabulary. Routine end: R01 'How to simplify expression with exponents', R12 'Differentiate y=e^{ax^3}', R24 'Finding minima and maxima', R34 and R41 and R47 (same multiple-choice 9! item, with R34 stating 'Option (A) is correct'), R13 with a boxed final fraction. Specialist end: R42 (Levy collapse, generic filters), R46 (Kronecker-Weber, cyclotomic fields), R02 (Poincare-Hopf on fibre bundles), R40 (orbit of a diagonal matrix under O_3). Tagged mixed because question difficulty plausibly also shifts what counts as a satisfying answer.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of question the answer is attached to, and the size and composition of the crowd such a question draws

proposals.name: Informal affective typography, interjections and sign-offs
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of informal affective typography in the answer. Count: exclamation marks, especially runs of them; capitalised excitement or interjections ('AHAAA!', 'Well, jolly gosh!', 'ATTEMPT TO ORGANIZE THIS MATERIAL'); emoticons and kaomoji (':)', '^_^'); colloquial asides and jokes; parenthetical delight ('(Look!)'); friendly closings and signatures ('Cheers!', '-Shahar', 'I hope this helps', 'I hope this was helpful'); and chatty second-person filler ('Let's dig deeper', 'Not convinced yet? Ok'). 0 = entirely neutral academic typography with no exclamation, emoticon, joke or sign-off; 10 = several such markers spread through the text. Do NOT judge whether the informality is charming, unprofessional, or engaging; score only how much of it is present.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1, with a habit factor behind it. These marks cluster in a recognisable subset and are trivially detectable by a text model while saying nothing about whether the asker's own problem was resolved. R13 contains 'AHAAA!' and closes '...as our answer!!!!!', R17 contains 'Well, jolly gosh!' and closes 'Cheers! -Shahar', R37 closes 'I hope this helps ^_^', R43 closes with a 'PS' and ':)', R35 inserts '(Look!)' and 'not as much fun', R28 closes 'I hope this was helpful', R20 asks 'Not convinced yet? Ok, let's dig deeper'; R08, R36, R50 and R60 carry none. Purely a nuisance: register habit is not the asker's selection criterion.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's practice in this format and their register calibration to the venue

proposals.rationale: Formatting habits vary substantially across answers: R04, R35, R41, R45, and R49 use extensive structural or macro-heavy markup. These visible habits may track author practice and venue familiarity rather than mathematical quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Topic-specialization signature
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the paired question and answer visibly signal an elementary procedural topic or a specialized theoretical topic; do not judge the topic's importance or the answer's difficulty.
proposals.rationale: Routine exercises and specialist theory carry different vocabulary and audience signals. The contrast between R16 and R40 versus R41 and R49 shows how subject-matter context can predict reception through crowd and audience effects rather than answer quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of question and its audience

proposals.name: Era-marked conventions
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text contains notation, vocabulary, TeX idioms, or linking conventions associated with a particular period of the site's history; do not judge whether the conventions are modern or preferable.
proposals.rationale: Legacy macros, notation, and vocabulary can reveal when an answer was produced. Examples include R15, R21, R41, R45, and R49; such historical fingerprints can influence textual interpretation without measuring mathematical quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: site-era and historical conventions

proposals.name: Informal affective style
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the answer contains casual interjections, encouragement, humor, emoticons, exclamation runs, signatures, spelling quirks, or conversational asides; do not judge whether the tone is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Casual style is directly visible and may correlate with model behavior through register matching or formatting preferences. R05 uses jolly gosh and Cheers, R34 uses an emoticon, R48 uses AHAAA, and R60 uses friendly prompts; none is a mathematical-quality criterion.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Answer-length footprint
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent of the answer's textual length, explanatory verbosity, and structural expansiveness; do not judge whether more or less text is better.
proposals.rationale: Some entries are one-line hints or computations, while others contain extensive derivations and appendices. R03, R12, and R40 are terse, whereas R41 and R49 are highly expansive; length is a surface predictor rather than a quality criterion.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Validation of OP's Approach Together With Completion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly affirms the asker's original approach/partial work AND uses it as the direct foundation to complete the solution. Score 0 if it ignores the asker's attempt entirely and imposes a completely independent solution.
proposals.rationale: Askers are highly likely to accept answers that validate their thought process. The dense model favors answers that reassure the asker (e.g., 'Your work is correct') and guide them to the finish line, whereas the scorecard misses this interpersonal connection. Motivated by R01, R42, R52, R48.

proposals.name: Conversational Warmth and Encouragement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text uses a warm, encouraging, or highly conversational tone (e.g., enthusiastic phrasing, friendly sign-offs, active moral support). Score 0 if the tone is cold, purely formal, or condescending.
proposals.rationale: A supportive, friendly tone directly addresses the human element of asking a question, making the answer highly acceptable to the struggling asker. Motivated by R06, R55.

proposals.name: Highly Targeted Brevity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is exceptionally concise (1-3 sentences or a single equation) and flawlessly resolves the exact bottleneck without unnecessary fluff. Score 0 if it contains massive walls of text, overly long derivations, or broad tangents.
proposals.rationale: Askers often prefer a direct, instantly satisfying answer over a comprehensive treatise. The dense model perceives this directness, while the scorecard likely rewards length and comprehensiveness. Motivated by R03, R07, R23, R42.

proposals.name: Diagnosis of Misconception Together With Fix
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer pinpoints the exact logical, computational, or conceptual error in the asker's formulation AND explains how to fix it. Score 0 if it simply provides a standard proof from scratch without diagnosing why the asker was stuck.
proposals.rationale: Askers accept answers that unblock their specific mental hurdle. The dense model favors answers that fix the asker's broken logic rather than ignoring it to show off a textbook proof. Motivated by R20, R01.

proposals.name: Actionable Heuristics or Rules of Thumb
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer provides practical, strategic advice for tackling the problem (e.g., 'draw the picture first' or 'try looking at the OEIS'). Score 0 if it only provides raw algebraic manipulation with no strategic guidance.
proposals.rationale: An answer that teaches the asker *how* to fish is highly prized. The dense model recognizes the value of tactical advice, while the scorecard misses it by focusing only on formal math. Motivated by R22, R34.

proposals.name: Socratic Prompting and Interactivity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer deliberately leaves a specific, small piece of work for the asker to complete, or actively prompts the asker to solve a related practice problem. Score 0 if it spoon-feeds the entire solution with no interactive engagement.
proposals.rationale: Engaging the asker directly by making them finish a step or try an example fosters learning, which askers often appreciate and reward. Motivated by R06, R14, R50.

proposals.name: Elegance via Trivial Counterexample
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer resolves a 'prove or disprove' prompt using a simple, immediate, and trivial-to-verify counterexample. Score 0 if it uses a long, convoluted argument to prove or disprove the claim.
proposals.rationale: Counterexamples that are immediately obvious provide instant clarity and relief to the asker, explaining why the dense model favors them over brute-force explanations. Motivated by R23, R51.

proposals.name: Practical Tooling or Resource Pointers
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly directs the user to a practical tool (like OEIS, computational software, or code) to solve their problem. Score 0 if there are no practical resource recommendations.
proposals.rationale: Pointing an asker to the exact database sequence or code snippet that solves their problem provides lasting utility that pure math derivations lack. Motivated by R26, R34, R19.

proposals.name: Explicit Hint Over Full Solution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer deliberately restricts full detail to encourage thinking, explicitly framing itself as a hint. Score 0 if it provides the full solution with no restrictions.
proposals.rationale: When askers want a nudge rather than a complete spoon-feeding, they accept well-crafted hints. The scorecard likely penalizes incomplete solutions, while the dense model perceives their pedagogical value. Motivated by R12, R14, R29.

proposals.name: Dismissiveness Toward Alternatives
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer contains condescending language dismissing other answers, methods, or the asker's intellect (e.g., 'way too complicated', 'jolly gosh'). Score 0 if the tone is respectful and purely mathematical.
proposals.rationale: Askers are alienated by arrogant or condescending tones, explaining why the dense model ranks them low even if the math is technically rigorous. Motivated by R04, R19, R13.

proposals.name: Transparent Algebraic Continuity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if every algebraic step is shown explicitly and sequentially without skipping, allowing the asker to follow along line-by-line. Score 0 if the answer hides massive amounts of work using phrases like 'After a long calculation'.
proposals.rationale: Askers trying to understand a specific step get frustrated by opaque algebraic leaps. The dense model favors answers that hold the asker's hand through the math. Motivated by R24, R38, R54.

proposals.name: Intuitive Reframing Together With Trivial Conclusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer uses a clever substitution, change of perspective, or analogy that makes the mathematical conclusion 'obviously true' or trivial to see. Score 0 if it brute-forces the original formulation with dense math.
proposals.rationale: Reframing a problem to make it trivial provides a 'eureka' moment for the asker, which is highly likely to be accepted over a grueling algebraic grind. Motivated by R28, R09, R18.

proposals.name: Explicit Multiple-Choice Conclusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer clearly concludes which specific multiple-choice option (e.g., 'Option A') or exact formatted answer is correct. Score 0 if it ends with a general formula or does not match the requested output format.
proposals.rationale: If the asker provides options, explicitly selecting the correct one leaves zero ambiguity, perfectly satisfying their prompt. Motivated by R05, R07.

proposals.name: Excessive Meta-Commentary or Apologies
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer contains large disclaimers, apologies, or explanations about the post itself rather than the math (e.g., 'This is not an answer but...'). Score 0 if it gets straight to the mathematical point.
proposals.rationale: Answers prefaced with apologies or rambling meta-commentary often fail to directly satisfy the asker's urgency, explaining the dense model's low scores for these items. Motivated by R37, R58.

proposals.name: Real-World or Everyday Analogies
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text maps the mathematical concept to an everyday real-world scenario (e.g., engineering grids, clocks, money). Score 0 if the explanation relies strictly on formal mathematical objects and notation.
proposals.rationale: Abstract concepts become accessible when grounded in reality. Askers highly appreciate analogies that make intimidating math relatable, a nuance missed by the scorecard. Motivated by R06, R40, R43.

proposals.name: Extreme text brevity in prose
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the answer is extremely short in terms of English prose, consisting almost entirely of equations or brief mathematical statements with zero conversational transitions or explanatory text. Do not judge if this brevity is good or bad, simply measure the lack of connecting prose.
proposals.rationale: Rows R05 and R07 consist almost entirely of equations or single sentences (e.g., 'Your computation looks fine.'). A dense model might perceive this terse, highly declarative style as authoritative (mapping to high-reputation users), while a scorecard model penalizes it for lacking step-by-step detail.
proposals.upstream_parent: Author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Explicit references to existing thread
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the text explicitly references the original poster (e.g., 'OP's technique'), other answers (e.g., 'the other answer'), or specific users (e.g., '@user'), indicating it is responding to an existing thread rather than standing alone. Do not judge the accuracy or usefulness of the reference.
proposals.rationale: Rows R03 and R22 explicitly state 'Using OP's second technique' and 'The other answer has roughly the right idea'. These textual fingerprints indicate the answer arrived later in the thread. Dense models often miss the context value of these additions, while scorecards may reward the synthesized completeness.
proposals.upstream_parent: Position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Conversational or narrative framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the answer contains conversational filler, narrative asides, or first-person commentary (e.g., 'jolly gosh', 'Just look at this equation', disclaimers) that is extraneous to the mathematical derivation itself. Do not judge if this tone is appropriate, simply measure how much is present.
proposals.rationale: Rows R55 and R59 use highly conversational framing ('Well, jolly gosh!' and 'Just look at this equation for a few seconds.'). This stylistic choice can inflate scorecard metrics for 'engagement' but might cause a dense model to rank it lower if it dilutes the mathematical focus.
proposals.upstream_parent: Answerer's relationship to the reader

proposals.name: Reliance on external computation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the answer relies on pointing the user to external databases (like OEIS), software (like GAP, Mathematica), or contains non-mathematical code blocks as the primary proof mechanism. Do not judge if using these tools is correct; only measure their prominence in the text.
proposals.rationale: Rows R40 and R48 essentially outsource the solution to OEIS and GAP code, respectively. This is an upstream process shortcut rather than an inherent textual quality of a mathematical derivation, creating divergences between models that parse text semantics vs. those that score structural completeness.
proposals.upstream_parent: Process dynamics / availability of computation tools

proposals.name: Journal-article structural formality
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the answer mimics a formal mathematical publication, using structural markers like 'Lemma', 'Proof', 'Claim', 'Theorem', or defining custom LaTeX macros at the beginning. Do not judge the quality of the formatting, only measure the level of formal structural mimicry.
proposals.rationale: Rows R01 and R43 use formal sections like 'Lemma 1' and define macros at the top. Dense models might associate this rigid academic style with the accepted answers of complex questions, while scorecards might penalize it for poor readability or being overly dense for a casual forum.
proposals.upstream_parent: Author's seniority / academic practice

proposals.name: Explicit mention of multiple own answers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the text explicitly identifies itself as a secondary or alternative answer to the same question by the same author (e.g., 'I post this answer separately', 'This second answer', 'my other solution'). Do not judge if this is a good practice, only measure if it occurs.
proposals.rationale: Rows R14 and R52 explicitly state 'I post this answer separately' and 'my other solution below'. This is a platform-specific quirk of answering a question multiple times, which alters the structural assumptions of the text but is not an indicator of the underlying math's intrinsic quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: Position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Explicit inline edit markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the text contains explicit inline edit annotations (e.g., 'EDIT:', 'EDIT 1.', 'Update:') indicating that the original text was retroactively modified in response to comments or further thought. Do not judge the content of the edit, only the presence of the marker.
proposals.rationale: Rows R02 and R18 contain explicit 'EDIT 1.' and 'EDIT' sections. These markers reflect an ongoing collaborative or corrective process over time, acting as a nuisance proxy for engagement rather than a measure of standalone mathematical clarity.
proposals.upstream_parent: Process dynamics on the receiving side

proposals.name: Explicit Hint or partial solution format
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the text explicitly frames itself as a 'hint' or deliberately leaves the main derivation or final computation for the asker to complete, rather than providing a fully worked solution. Do not judge the pedagogical value of the hint, only measure how much it withholds a full solution.
proposals.rationale: Rows R08 and R58 simply say 'Hint:' and provide a starting point. Dense models often map these terse hints to high acceptance rates (if given by experienced users resolving the asker's specific block), while scorecards strictly penalize them for lacking step-by-step resolution.
proposals.upstream_parent: Answerer's relationship to the reader

proposals.name: Enthusiastic or casual punctuation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT of casual or enthusiastic punctuation marks used outside of mathematical notation, such as exclamation points (!), multiple question marks (??), or emoticons/kaomoji (^_^). Do not judge if this punctuation makes the text better or worse, simply count its prominence.
proposals.rationale: Rows R40 and R44 use emoticons like '^_^' and multiple exclamation marks ('!!!!!!'). Dense models often penalize this unprofessional surface typography as low-effort, while scorecards might ignore it entirely if the underlying mathematical criteria are satisfied.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Over-explanation of basic prerequisites
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on the EXTENT to which the answer includes definitions or explanations of basic prerequisites that are far simpler than the question's subject matter implies (e.g., defining a basic field, explaining what a set is, explaining basic algebra rules). Do not judge if this is helpful, only measure the presence of basic pedagogical digressions.
proposals.rationale: Row R20 explains the definition of a field in exhaustive detail just to explain notation, and Row R50 gives an overly simplified 'engineering' explanation of basic powers. This verbosity can bloat scorecard scores (rewarding 'thoroughness') while a dense model might not perceive it as the direct, focused answer preferred by the asker.
proposals.upstream_parent: Answerer's relationship to the reader

proposals.name: Asker-method continuation over replacement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer picks up the asker's own method or notation and carries it through to a result; score 0 if it ignores the asker's approach entirely and substitutes an unrelated technique.
proposals.rationale: R01 continues the asker's L'Hôpital computation line by line, and R05 completes the asker's logarithmic-differentiation approach before noting the chain rule shortcut. The scorecard likely rewards sophisticated alternative proofs (e.g. R02, R39) that do not engage with what the asker actually tried.

proposals.name: Sophistication-level match to question
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the mathematical machinery is calibrated to the question's apparent level—simple tools for simple questions, advanced tools only for advanced questions. Score 0 if the answer is wildly over-powered (research-level machinery for a homework problem) or under-powered.
proposals.rationale: R06 gives a one-line counterexample perfectly matched to a basic set-theory question, while R43 uses only exponent laws for a simplification question. The scorecard appears to over-credit sophisticated machinery regardless of fit (R02 deploys Lie-group orbit theory for a question the asker framed in elementary terms, R07 is a research-level blog-post-style answer).

proposals.name: Immediate verdict before explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the very first sentence or two states a clear conclusion (the answer is X, your work is correct, use this theorem). Score 0 if the reader must wade through setup or derivation before learning the verdict.
proposals.rationale: R01 opens with 'It should be used,' R05 concludes 'So your work is correct,' and R42 immediately lists candidate numbers. Dense-low answers like R02 and R33 bury the conclusion under long expositions.

proposals.name: Pinpoint diagnosis of asker's specific error
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer identifies the exact step where the asker went wrong and names the conceptual or computational mistake. Score 0 if it gives no diagnosis or only a vague one.
proposals.rationale: R10 pinpoints two distinct counting errors in the asker's birthday-probability reasoning, and R01 notes 'there may be some little mistakes in your computation' then shows the corrected lines. Answers like R33 and R51 never diagnose any error because they do not engage with the asker's work at all.

proposals.name: Concision without information loss
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is as short as possible while remaining complete and correct. Score 0 if it is padded with tangents, excessive generality, or unnecessary derivation.
proposals.rationale: R59 establishes the series-integral equality in four lines, and R06 disproves the claim with a single counterexample. The scorecard seems to over-credit length and thoroughness—R07 and R51 are extremely long posts that a question-asker would likely find overwhelming.

proposals.name: Standalone independence from other answers
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is fully self-contained and understandable without reading any other answer. Score 0 if it is explicitly framed as a correction, supplement, or addendum to another answer and makes little sense alone.
proposals.rationale: R01, R05, and R38 each stand completely alone. By contrast, R18 begins 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to Robert Israel's answer,' R24 is entirely about fixing another answer's edge cases, and R32 says '@supinf showed us a nice set of examples. I think the proof can be simplified.'

proposals.name: Supportive and patient register
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tone is warm, encouraging, and treats the asker's confusion with respect. Score 0 if the tone is dismissive, condescending, or coldly perfunctory.
proposals.rationale: R40 says 'You are lucky here because of the choice of f' and adds a friendly PS, while R53 walks the asker through examples with 'You try one.' Dense-low answers like R27 ('You are overcomplicating it') and R49 ('The other answers are way too complicated') adopt a more dismissive stance.

proposals.name: Concrete numerical or visual instantiation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer includes specific numbers, computed values, plots, or diagrams that make the abstract tangible. Score 0 if it is entirely symbolic with no concrete instance.
proposals.rationale: R53 works through specific time divisions (7:41, 16:56, 27:32), R35 includes simulation histograms, and R47 computes the factorization of 9! explicitly. Dense-low answers like R02 and R45 are entirely formal with no grounding examples.

proposals.name: Notation continuity with the question
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer uses exactly the same variable names, symbols, and formatting conventions as the question. Score 0 if it introduces entirely new notation without bridging to the asker's.
proposals.rationale: R20 explicitly says 'ATTEMPT TO ORGANIZE THIS MATERIAL' and reuses the asker's own tensor expressions, and R46 works with the asker's a, b, c notation throughout. Dense-low answers like R02 introduce their own macro definitions and notation systems (e.g. $\newcommand{\O}{\mathcal{O}}$).

proposals.name: Affirmation of correct work before correction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer first acknowledges what the asker got right, then addresses what needs fixing. Score 0 if it jumps straight to corrections or never acknowledges any correct element.
proposals.rationale: R05 states 'So your work is correct' before noting the chain rule would be easier, and R21 opens with 'Your computation looks fine.' This validation-first pattern is absent from dense-low items like R49, which dismisses prior work as 'completely overkill.'

proposals.name: Interactive invitation to the asker
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer includes a practice problem, a 'you try this,' a directed question, or another element that invites the asker to participate actively. Score 0 if it is purely one-directional information delivery.
proposals.rationale: R53 includes 'You try one: What is 9:51 divided by two? (answer at end),' and R55 provides a hint then hides the full proof behind a reveal, inviting the asker to attempt it first. No dense-low item includes such interactive elements.

proposals.name: Scope discipline: answers what was asked
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer addresses exactly what was asked—no more, no less. Score 0 if it wanders into extensive unrequested generalizations, philosophical digressions, or meta-discussion.
proposals.rationale: R43 answers a simplification question in five lines of algebra and stops, and R44 proves the specific polynomial claim concisely. Dense-low items like R54 ('This is an interesting observation, but imho this is a case where there is less than meets the eye') and R51 (a multi-page exposition on forcing) range far beyond what was asked.

proposals.name: Rapid result extractability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a reader can extract the key numerical or symbolic answer within a few seconds of scanning. Score 0 if the answer's conclusion is buried, implicit, or requires working through the entire derivation to locate.
proposals.rationale: R42 states 'The possible numbers are 5,11,17,23,29,35' immediately, and R59 displays the series equality in a single displayed equation. Dense-low answers like R33 and R37 require reading through long developments before the conclusion is reachable.

proposals.name: Disposition of method choice for the asker
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer either uses the single most natural method for the asker's level or briefly explains why the chosen approach is the right one for this problem. Score 0 if it presents an advanced method with no discussion of why it is appropriate or what simpler alternatives exist.
proposals.rationale: R01 confirms L'Hôpital is the right tool for the asker's limit, and R05 notes 'Of course, this would be more easily done with the chain rule,' guiding the asker toward the simpler path. Dense-low items like R04 ('using one of my favorite techniques') and R08 present specific methods without connecting to the asker's likely toolkit.

proposals.name: Absence of self-positioning meta-talk
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer reads as a direct response to the question with no framing about its own role. Score 0 if it opens with meta-commentary like 'This is not an answer,' 'Here is yet another way,' 'The other answers are wrong,' or 'Expanding on a comment.'
proposals.rationale: R05, R09, and R38 dive directly into mathematical content. Dense-low items are laden with self-positioning: R02 ('This second answer gives a shorter proof, more algebraic, which does not expand on your ideas'), R18 ('This is not an answer to the question but a complement'), R49 ('The other answers are way too complicated'), and R52 ('Clive's answer is already a good one, I just wanted to add').

proposals.name: Total verbosity and length
proposals.instruction: Score the overall length and verbosity of the answer, from extremely terse to extremely long-winded, accounting for words, equations, and elaborative prose. Do not judge whether the length is helpful or excessive.
proposals.rationale: Items such as R01, R02, R03, R17, and R52 are extremely long, whereas R22, R46, R49, and R55 are very short. The scorecard likely rewards elaboration, but total verbosity is not itself whether the asker marked the answer accepted.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's verbosity and desire to be comprehensive

proposals.name: Site-specific LaTeX macro density
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer uses advanced, site-specific, or custom LaTeX constructs such as \\newcommand, \\def, \\fitch, \\operatorname, or heavy display environments, as opposed to plain text or basic inline math. Do not judge whether the formatting is good.
proposals.rationale: R01, R02, R03, R41, and R60 use heavy custom macros, while R04, R22, R36, and R55 use little to none. This markup density reflects author practice and may bias models, but it is not the acceptedness itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and familiarity with the site markup

proposals.name: References to prior answers or comments
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer explicitly references other answers, comments, or prior posts, using phrases like 'the other answer', 'as suggested by', or 'based on a comment by'. Do not judge whether referencing others is good.
proposals.rationale: R05, R10, R27, R38, and R42 explicitly reference other answers or comments, indicating they are later entries; dense_high_card_low items like R04, R15, R46, and R55 do not. This position tell likely affects the dense model but is not the asker's selection.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Direct engagement with asker's working
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer directly addresses the asker's specific attempt, quotes the asker's variables, or comments on the asker's computation. Do not judge whether such engagement is effective.
proposals.rationale: R15, R22, R24, and R25 directly address the asker's own working, whereas R01, R02, R48, and R52 speak to a general audience. Such asker-specific engagement may correlate with acceptance but is not the acceptance event.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's relationship to the reader

proposals.name: Structural headers and labeled edits
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer uses explicit structural organization such as section headers, 'Claim', 'Proof', 'Definition', 'Case 1', or labeled edits like 'EDIT 1'. Do not judge whether the structure is well done.
proposals.rationale: R01 (Definitions), R02 (Basic computations, Claim), R17 (EDIT 1), and R28 (Lemma 1) show heavy structure, while R04, R22, R36, and R46 do not. Structural formatting impresses the scorecard but is not whether the answer was accepted.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's formatting practice and editing history

proposals.name: Conversational or first-person framing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of first-person voice, hedging phrases such as 'I think' or 'I believe', and conversational asides. Do not judge whether the tone is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R01, R02, R11, R33, and R52 use first-person and hedging, while R09, R15, R36, and R55 are impersonal. This register may influence model scores but is not the acceptedness.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's register and seniority

proposals.name: Terse declarative delivery
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer is flat, declarative, and presents the result immediately without meta-commentary or elaborate setup. Do not judge whether being terse is good.
proposals.rationale: R22, R46, R49, and R55 are terse and declarative, whereas R01, R02, R10, and R48 have long preambles. Terse delivery may be favored by the dense model but is not acceptance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's willingness to be terse and practice in the format

proposals.name: Punctuation enthusiasm and informal closings
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of exclamation runs, informal sign-offs such as 'Cheers!' or 'I hope this was helpful', emoticons, or emphatic typography. Do not judge whether such markers are good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('AHAAA!', '!!!!!'), R33 ('Cheers!'), R50 ('^_^'), and R26 ('I hope this was helpful') show informal markers, while most dense_low_card_high items lack them. This is a pure surface tell that may bias a model without reflecting acceptance.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Citations to external resources
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer cites external tools, databases, or literature, such as OEIS, GAP, WolframAlpha, arXiv, or blog posts. Do not judge whether citations are accurate or useful.
proposals.rationale: R18 (GAP code), R33 (WolframAlpha), R50 (OEIS), R52 (Wolfram Alpha), and R58 (references) cite resources, while R04, R15, R22, R36, and R55 do not. Citations may impress the scorecard but are not the asker's acceptance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's technical environment and prior knowledge

proposals.name: Formal notation density versus prose
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer is dominated by dense formal mathematical notation and multi-line equations with minimal intervening explanatory prose. Do not judge whether the formalism is correct or helpful.
proposals.rationale: R03, R12, R17, R41, and R58 are dominated by dense formalism, while R04, R22, R25, and R26 are more prose or simple notation. Topic-driven formality likely affects both models but is not whether the answer was accepted.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of question the answer is attached to
